title: Exam Cram
subject: Lymphoid System
introMarkdown: A compact explanatory review of lymphatic transport, lymphoid anatomy, innate and adaptive immunity, immune cells, antibodies, and memory. Use Quick Scan when you want the most concise terms and pathways.

sections.title: Three Core Roles
sections.markdown:
The lymphatic and lymphoid systems perform **three connected functions**:

1. **Fluid recovery:** Returns excess **interstitial fluid** and associated proteins to the blood, helping prevent edema.
2. **Immune surveillance/defense:** Transports immune cells and antigen-bearing material; lymphoid organs and tissues support immune-cell development, activation, and filtration.
3. **Dietary-fat transport:** Intestinal **lacteals** collect chylomicrons; lipid-rich **chyle** travels through lymphatic vessels toward the venous blood.

**Also remember:** Lymphopoiesis means lymphocyte production; the lymphoid system helps produce, maintain, and distribute lymphocytes. The immune system's functions extend beyond the physical lymphatic vessels.

sections.title: Lymph, Interstitial Fluid, and Capillaries
sections.markdown:
- **Blood plasma:** Liquid component of blood within blood vessels.
- **Interstitial fluid:** Extracellular fluid between tissue cells.
- **Lymph:** Interstitial fluid after it enters a lymphatic vessel; typically lower in protein than blood plasma in many tissues.
- **Initial lymphatic capillaries:** Blind-ended pockets with larger lumens and thinner, more permeable walls than typical blood capillaries.
- **Overlapping endothelial flaps:** Open when outside tissue pressure exceeds inside lymphatic pressure, permitting entry; tend to close when pressure reverses.
- **Blood capillaries:** Exchange water and solutes with surrounding tissue as part of an arterial–venous network; **lymphatic capillaries begin blindly** rather than connecting two sides of a blood circuit.
- **Anchoring filaments and incomplete basement membrane:** Help initial lymphatic capillaries admit fluid and larger material.

**Route:** Blood plasma → fluid filtered into tissues (interstitial fluid) → initial lymphatic capillary (lymph) → collecting vessels.

**Caution:** One-way entry does **not** mean pathogens are physically incapable of ever leaving lymphatic channels or spreading through the body.

sections.title: Valves and Lymph Propulsion
sections.markdown:
- **Why valves?** Lymph pressure is low; valves prevent backflow and support movement toward the large venous trunks.
- **Propulsion:** Intrinsic lymphatic smooth-muscle contractions, skeletal-muscle compression, respiratory pressure changes, and nearby pulsations.
- **Comparison with veins:** Collecting lymphatics resemble small veins, often with more closely spaced valves; no central lymphatic heart exists.
- **Lymphedema:** Swelling from impaired lymph drainage; fluid-recovery failure is not the only possible cause of edema.

**Remember:** Initial lymphatic capillary *entry flaps* admit tissue fluid; collecting-vessel *valves* prevent reverse flow farther downstream.

sections.title: Right Duct, Thoracic Duct, and Trunks
sections.markdown:
| Structure | Territory or input | Venous return |
|---|---|---|
| **Right lymphatic duct** | Right upper quadrant: right head/neck, right upper limb, right upper thorax | Right venous angle (right internal jugular–subclavian junction) |
| **Thoracic duct** | Left upper quadrant **plus essentially the entire body inferior to the diaphragm** | Left venous angle (left internal jugular–subclavian junction) |
| **Cisterna chyli** | Variable enlarged collecting region near the lower thoracic duct, commonly receiving intestinal and lumbar trunks | Continues into thoracic duct |

**Three principal right-sided lymphatic trunks:**

1. **Right jugular trunk** — right head and neck.
2. **Right subclavian trunk** — right upper limb.
3. **Right bronchomediastinal trunk** — right thoracic structures.

**Six commonly grouped trunks contributing to the thoracic drainage system:** **Left jugular, left subclavian, left bronchomediastinal, right lumbar, left lumbar, and intestinal.** The left-sided upper trunks join the thoracic duct system near its termination; the lumbar and intestinal drainage contributes inferiorly, often through the cisterna chyli. Anatomical variants exist.

**Anatomical distinction:** Lymph returns to venous blood at or near the junctions of the internal jugular and subclavian veins (the venous angles), not into an artery.

sections.title: Three Course-Defined Lymphoid Organs vs Tissues
sections.markdown:
**Three commonly illustrated encapsulated lymphoid organs:** **lymph nodes, thymus, spleen**.

- **Encapsulated lymphoid organ:** Organized lymphoid tissue with a connective-tissue **capsule**.
- **Nonencapsulated or less distinctly encapsulated lymphoid tissue:** Lymphocyte-rich tissue or nodules without a complete separate capsule; includes many **tonsillar**, **MALT**, and **Peyer's patch** sites.
- **Primary lymphoid sites (functional classification):** **Bone marrow** (blood-cell and B-cell development) and **thymus** (T-cell maturation).
- **Secondary lymphoid sites:** **Lymph nodes, spleen, and organized mucosal lymphoid tissues** where mature lymphocytes encounter antigen.

**Classification note:** Bone marrow is also a **primary lymphoid organ** in standard immunology. The three listed above are a particular anatomical grouping, not an exhaustive definition of lymphoid organs.

sections.title: Lymph Node Flow and Identification
sections.markdown:
**Fluid pathway to memorize:** **Afferent lymphatic** → **subcapsular sinus** → **cortical/trabecular sinuses** → **medullary sinuses** → **efferent lymphatic** → larger collecting vessels.

- **Afferent = arrives:** Usually enter around the convex surface of the node.
- **Efferent = exits:** Usually leave at the **hilum**.
- **Capsule:** Outer connective-tissue covering; **trabeculae** extend inward.
- **Hilum:** Indentation where major blood vessels pass and efferent lymphatics leave.
- **Outer cortex:** Lymphoid follicles, predominantly **B-cell** regions.
- **Paracortex/deep cortex:** Predominantly **T-cell** region; important for antigen presentation.
- **Medulla:** Medullary **cords** containing plasma cells, B cells and macrophages; nearby medullary **sinuses** conduct lymph.
- **Germinal center:** Active region in certain B-cell follicles where activated B cells proliferate and undergo selection/differentiation.
- **Role of nodes:** Filter lymph and increase encounters among antigen, antigen-presenting cells, and appropriate lymphocytes.

**Important distinction:** B-cell-rich cortex and T-cell-rich paracortex describe **regions**. Lymph fluid travels through interconnected **sinuses** rather than literally flowing from one lymphocyte population into another.

sections.title: B Cells, T Cells, NK Cells, and Lymphopoiesis
sections.markdown:
| Class | Site of development/maturation | Main defense |
|---|---|---|
| **B lymphocyte** | Develops and matures primarily in **bone marrow** | **Adaptive, humoral/antibody-mediated** immunity; plasma cells secrete antibodies |
| **T lymphocyte** | Precursors arise in marrow; maturation and selection in **thymus** | **Adaptive, cell-mediated** immunity and coordination |
| **Natural killer (NK) cell** | Hematopoietic lineage, developing mainly in marrow-associated environments | **Innate** surveillance and killing of certain abnormal or infected cells |

- **Helper T cell (CD4):** Coordinates immune responses via cytokines and contact signals; supports suitable B-cell responses.
- **Cytotoxic T cell (CD8):** Kills appropriately recognized infected or abnormal host cells.
- **Regulatory T cell:** Helps restrain inappropriate activation; older terminology includes *suppressor* T cells.
- **Plasma cell:** An activated, differentiated **B cell** specialized to secrete antibodies.
- **Memory cells:** Long-lived antigen-experienced B/T cells that support future responses.

**Question needing clarification:** The study guide asks for a hormone controlling **B-cell differentiation**, but the provided material does not identify such a hormone. **Thymosins** are associated with **T-cell** development in the thymus, not with B-cell differentiation. Do not substitute thymosin as an unsupported B-cell answer.

sections.title: Thymus, Blood–Thymus Barrier, and Involution
sections.markdown:
- **Location:** Anterior/superior mediastinal region, especially prominent early in life.
- **Architecture:** Two lobes; fibrous septa divide tissue into lobules with darker **cortex** and paler **medulla**.
- **Function:** Supports T-cell differentiation, maturation, and selection; it is **not** a lymph-node-style filter of incoming lymph.
- **Blood–thymus barrier:** Specialized capillary and epithelial arrangements in the cortex that help protect developing thymocytes from uncontrolled exposure to circulating antigens.
- **Reticular epithelial cells (thymic epithelial cells):** Contribute to thymic environment and blood–thymus barrier; support developing T cells.
- **Thymic corpuscles (Hassall corpuscles):** Characteristic concentrically arranged epithelial structures in the **medulla**.
- **Thymosins:** Traditional collective label for thymic hormones/signals associated with T-cell development.
- **Involution:** Gradual loss of thymic functional mass with increasing fatty replacement, especially after puberty; does not instantly eliminate mature T cells.

**Selection principle:** Positive and negative selection establish useful MHC recognition while reducing strongly self-reactive T cells.

sections.title: Spleen: Red/White Pulp and Blood Path
sections.markdown:
- **Largest lymphoid organ**; in the **left upper abdomen** near ribs **9–11**.
- **Primary function:** Filters **blood**, unlike lymph nodes that filter **lymph**.
- **Red pulp:** Blood-filled sinusoids and reticular tissue rich in RBCs and macrophages; removes aged/damaged erythrocytes and recovers iron.
- **White pulp:** Lymphocyte-rich tissue organized around arteries; supports blood-borne antigen recognition.
- **Capsule/trabeculae:** Fibrous support and routes for vessels.
- **Hilum:** Entry/exit for **splenic artery and vein**.

**Simplified splenic blood-flow sequence:** Splenic artery → trabecular arteries → central arteries associated with white pulp → smaller arterioles/capillary pathways → red-pulp cords and sinusoids → veins → trabecular veins → splenic vein.

**Clinical association:** Traumatic **splenic rupture** can produce dangerous internal bleeding; **splenectomy** is surgical removal and affects immune protection against certain infections.

sections.title: Tonsils, Peyer's Patches, and MALT
sections.markdown:
- **MALT:** Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue; immune surveillance at mucosal surfaces.
- **GALT:** Gut-associated lymphoid tissue; **BALT:** bronchus-associated; **NALT:** nasal-associated.
- **Tonsils:** **Palatine** near the oropharynx; **pharyngeal** in nasopharynx; **lingual** at tongue base. Together contribute to **Waldeyer's ring**.
- **Tonsillar grouping:** Two palatine tonsils, a pharyngeal tonsil, and lingual tonsillar tissue; the latter may contain multiple nodules rather than forming exactly two discrete organs.
- **Peyer's patches:** Aggregated lymphoid nodules, especially in the **ileum**; monitor intestinal antigens and participate in mucosal defense.
- **Appendix:** Rich in lymphoid tissue; inflammatory infection can cause appendicitis.
- **Germinal center:** Proliferating and differentiating activated B cells within some follicles; present in nodes and other secondary lymphoid tissues.

sections.title: Seven Nonspecific Defenses — Instructor's Exact List
sections.markdown:
1. **Physical barriers:** Skin, mucosa, and secretions prevent entry.
2. **Phagocytes:** Neutrophils/macrophages ingest microbes and debris.
3. **Immunological surveillance:** NK cells detect and kill certain stressed/abnormal cells.
4. **Interferons:** Promote antiviral defenses in neighboring cells.
5. **Complement system:** Opsonization, inflammation, membrane attack.
6. **Inflammation:** Recruits defenses, changes vascular flow, helps contain injury.
7. **Fever:** Systemic temperature-set-point response, sometimes hindering pathogens.

**Innate/nonspecific:** Rapid mechanisms that do not require prior antigen-specific clonal memory. These defenses can still recognize distinct microbial patterns; “nonspecific” does not mean indiscriminate.

sections.title: NK Cytotoxicity, Interferons, and Complement
sections.markdown:
**NK-cell attack:** Recognition/activation at a suspicious target → release of **perforin** (helps deliver cytotoxic material) and **granzymes** (induce cell-death pathways) → apoptosis of susceptible target. NK cells contribute to surveillance of virus-infected and malignant cells; recognition is regulated and not indiscriminate.

**Interferons:** Cytokines released in response to infection (including by virus-infected cells); bind receptors on other cells → expression of antiviral response proteins → reduced viral replication under suitable conditions.

**Complement:** Plasma-protein cascade activated by different triggers, including antigen–antibody complexes in the **classical pathway**. High yield:

- **C3b:** Major **opsonin**, coating targets to increase phagocytic uptake.
- **C3a/C5a:** Promote inflammation; **C5a** is also important for leukocyte recruitment.
- **C5b–C9:** **Membrane attack complex (MAC)**, which can damage susceptible target membranes.

**Distinguish:** **Neutralization** blocks a toxin or pathogen from interacting with its target; **opsonization** marks a target for easier phagocytosis; **MAC** attacks membranes.

sections.title: Four Cardinal Signs, Inflammation, and Fever
sections.markdown:
| Classical sign | Meaning | Typical mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| **Rubor** | Redness | Increased local blood flow |
| **Calor** | Heat | Increased blood flow and local activity |
| **Tumor** | Swelling | Fluid leakage/accumulation |
| **Dolor** | Pain | Inflammatory mediators, injury, pressure |

- **Inflammation:** Local coordinated response to injury, microbes, heat, chemicals, etc.; contains threats, recruits immune cells, promotes repair.
- **Mast-cell mediators:** Including **histamine**, which contributes to vasodilation and increased vascular permeability.
- **Phagocyte recruitment:** Neutrophils and monocytes respond to local signals.
- **Fever:** Endogenous/exogenous **pyrogens** influence hypothalamic temperature regulation; the body temporarily defends a higher temperature set point.

**Temperature note:** Some introductory examples use approximately **37.2°C/99°F** as a reference, but fever thresholds vary with measurement site and clinical context. The four classic inflammation terms are **rubor, calor, tumor, and dolor**.

sections.title: Innate vs Adaptive; Active vs Passive Immunity
sections.markdown:
| Distinction | Meaning | Representative example |
|---|---|---|
| **Innate immunity** | Rapid defenses without antigen-specific clonal memory | Barriers, phagocytes, NK cells, complement |
| **Adaptive immunity** | Antigen-specific B/T responses; capacity for memory | Plasma-cell antibodies, cytotoxic T cells |
| **Active acquired** | Your own response produces immune memory | Infection or vaccination |
| **Passive acquired** | Ready-made antibodies transferred to you; usually temporary | Maternal antibodies or administered immunoglobulin |

- **Natural active:** Response after exposure/infection.
- **Artificial/induced active:** Response after **vaccination**.
- **Natural passive:** Maternal antibodies via placenta and/or breast milk.
- **Artificial/induced passive:** Given immune globulin or other antibody preparation.
- **Four adaptive properties:** **Specificity, versatility, memory, tolerance.** Tolerance limits destructive reactions to self.

**Key comparison:** Innate versus adaptive describes the immune mechanism; active versus passive describes **how acquired protection is obtained**. NK cells belong to innate defense, not “passive immunity.”

sections.title: MHC I/CD8 vs MHC II/CD4
sections.markdown:
| Feature | **MHC I** | **MHC II** |
|---|---|---|
| **Typical cell location** | Nearly all **nucleated** cells | Professional antigen-presenting cells: dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells |
| **Peptide source** | Largely **intracellular** proteins | Largely material taken up from **outside** the cell |
| **Recognized by** | **CD8 cytotoxic T cells** | **CD4 helper T cells** |
| **Main consequence** | Appropriately activated CD8 cells may destroy infected/abnormal presenting host cells | Activated CD4 cells coordinate responses and can help B cells make antibodies |

**Mechanism to know:**

- **MHC I sequence:** Intracellular peptide → displayed on MHC I → recognition by an appropriately activated matching **CD8 T cell** → perforin/granzyme or other programmed-death pathways target the presenting cell.
- **MHC II sequence:** Extracellular material ingested and processed by an APC → peptide on **MHC II** → appropriate **CD4 helper T cell** activation → cytokine/contact signals support downstream cells, including B cells.
- **Necessary qualification:** Normal nucleated cells express MHC I. It is **not itself an abnormal-cell tag**. Recognition of a relevant peptide plus activation context matters.

sections.title: B-Cell Activation, Antibodies, and Five Ig Classes
sections.markdown:
**Common protein-antigen pathway:** B-cell receptor binds intact antigen → B cell processes/presents peptide on **MHC II** → matching activated helper T cell supplies appropriate help → **clonal expansion** → **plasma cells** (antibody secretion) and **memory B cells**.

- **Antigen:** A molecule that can be recognized by immune receptors.
- **Epitope / antigenic determinant:** The specific molecular feature contacted by a receptor or antibody.
- **Antibody / immunoglobulin:** Heavy and light chains; variable ends bind antigen, constant region mediates class-dependent effects.

| Class | Major association to memorize |
|---|---|
| **IgM** | Often the **first major secreted** class in a primary response; commonly pentameric when secreted |
| **IgG** | Major serum antibody in many systemic responses; prominent later and in many secondary responses; can cross placenta |
| **IgA** | Mucosal secretions: saliva, tears, mucus, breast milk; often dimeric in secretions |
| **IgE** | Allergic responses, mast-cell/basophil activation, certain antiparasitic defenses |
| **IgD** | Primarily a **B-cell surface receptor** with IgM on many naïve B cells |

**Clarification:** “Activated B cells” are not all plasma cells; some become memory B cells. Antibody binding **does not always cause direct destruction** without additional mechanisms.

sections.title: Antibody Actions, Titer, and Secondary Response
sections.markdown:
**Antibody effects:**

- **Neutralization:** Blocks binding or entry by toxins, viruses or microbes.
- **Opsonization:** Coats a target to improve phagocyte recognition/ingestion.
- **Agglutination:** Cross-links particles/cells into clumps; **precipitation** links soluble antigens into larger complexes.
- **Complement activation:** Certain bound immunoglobulins initiate the classical complement pathway.
- **Recruitment:** Fc-dependent actions help recruit immune effector cells and inflammatory responses.

**Antibody titer:** A measure of the amount or activity of antigen-specific antibodies in a sample, usually serum; method-dependent.

**Primary response:** First encounter; lag while suitable lymphocytes activate/expand; early IgM and later IgG are common patterns, with a relatively modest peak.

**Secondary response:** Later encounter; memory cells and sometimes pre-existing antibodies often yield a **faster, stronger, more prolonged** response, often with prominent IgG after class switching.

**Key association:** **Memory** explains the different responses, not a new type of general lymphatic vessel.

sections.title: Diseases, Anatomy Checklist, and Rapid Recall
sections.markdown:
**Selected immune disorders and conditions:**

- **Appendicitis:** Inflammation of the vermiform appendix, often associated with luminal obstruction and bacterial overgrowth; rupture may spread infection into the abdomen.
- **HIV/AIDS:** HIV targets cells expressing **CD4**, especially helper T cells; advanced untreated infection may severely impair immune defenses. HIV infection does not automatically mean AIDS, nor does a common cold inevitably kill an infected person.
- **Autoimmune disease:** Immune responses against self structures; may involve pathogenic T cells, antibodies, or both. Examples: **psoriasis, multiple sclerosis, Addison disease, type 1 diabetes**.

**Anatomy identification checklist:**

- Entire lymphatic distribution: cervical, axillary, lumbar, pelvic, inguinal node groups; upper/lower limb lymphatics.
- Venous angles, right lymphatic duct, thoracic duct, **cisterna chyli**.
- Lymph node: **capsule, trabecula, hilum, afferent/efferent vessels, subcapsular sinus, B-cell cortex, T-cell paracortex, medulla, germinal center**.
- Thymus: two lobes, lobules, **cortex, medulla, septa**, thymic corpuscles.
- Spleen: **diaphragmatic/visceral surfaces, hilum, splenic artery/vein, red and white pulp**.
- **Pharyngeal, palatine and lingual tonsils; Peyer's patches; appendix; MALT**.

**Last-minute associations:**

- **Lymph nodes filter lymph; spleen filters blood; thymus matures T cells; marrow develops B cells.**
- **Right duct = right upper quadrant; thoracic duct = the rest.**
- **Afferent arrives; efferent exits. B cells = cortex; T cells = paracortex.**
- **MHC I → CD8 → infected host-cell killing; MHC II → CD4 → helper coordination.**
- **IgM early, IgG systemic/secondary, IgA secretions, IgE allergy, IgD B-cell surface.**
- **Primary response slower; secondary response faster because of memory.**
- **Fluid balance + immune surveillance + dietary fat absorption = three lymphatic roles.**

**Study-guide note:** The B-cell differentiation hormone question remains unresolved by the supplied sources; see “B Cells, T Cells, NK Cells, and Lymphopoiesis” above.
